content: The presence of casts in the urine strongly indicates a urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis. Red blood cells (RBCs) in the urine are often associated with tumors of the urinary tract, which can cause gross hematuria, giving the urine a visibly bloody appearance. Similarly, urinary stones can lead to the presence of RBCs in the urine. It is essential to repeat a urinalysis after the stone has passed to rule out an underlying urologic malignancy. If RBCs persist in the urine after the stone has passed, a urologic evaluation is warranted. A Gram stain can be performed in the emergency room or clinic to determine the presence of infection. A negative Gram stain suggests sterile urine, while the presence of bacteria in an unspun urine specimen indicates infection. Most urinary tract infections are caused by Gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, although Gram-positive organisms can also be responsible. When urinary calculi are present, it is common to find crystals in the urine analysis, often accompanied by RBCs and white blood cells (WBCs). The shape of the crystals can help laboratory technicians identify their composition. Alkaline pH: Urine infected by urea-splitting bacteria, such as Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, often has an alkaline pH. Acidic pH: Acidic urine predisposes patients to the formation of uric acid stones. WBCs: The presence of WBCs indicates infection or inflammation caused by stones, while WBC casts strongly suggest a urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis. RBCs: Tumors of the urinary tract or stones can result in RBCs in the urine. Persistent RBCs after stone passage necessitate further urologic evaluation to exclude malignancy. A complete blood count (CBC) may reveal leukocytosis, which suggests an infectious etiology. Anemia or abnormal platelet counts may be observed in cases of bleeding urologic tumors. Elevated hematocrit levels may indicate dehydration. Leukocytosis: Suggests an infectious cause. Anemia and abnormal platelet counts: May be seen in bleeding urologic tumors. Elevated hematocrit: Indicates dehydration. Serum blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels can be elevated due to renal disease or dehydration. A BUN level greater than 10 times the serum creatinine level suggests dehydration, while a BUN-to-creatinine ratio of 10 or less indicates renal pathology. Elevated BUN: May result from renal disease or dehydration. BUN >10 times serum creatinine: Indicates dehydration. BUN-to-creatinine ratio ≤10: Suggests renal pathology. Serum creatinine levels directly reflect renal function. Elevated creatinine levels indicate impaired renal function, regardless of BUN levels. Abnormal creatinine levels may result from dehydration, obstruction, tumors, infarcts, bilateral renal disease, or solitary kidney disease. Elevated creatinine: Indicates impaired renal function. Abnormal levels: May result from dehydration, obstruction, tumors, infarcts, bilateral renal disease, or solitary kidney disease. Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, uric acid, and calcium levels may provide additional diagnostic information: Hyponatremia: Results from volume overload and may cause nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Hyperkalemia: Can lead to cardiac arrhythmias. Low serum bicarbonate: Indicates long-standing renal compromise, often accompanied by hyperkalemia. Serum uric acid and calcium levels: Measured in suspected cases of urinary calculi. A beta-hCG test is performed in females of reproductive age to confirm or rule out pregnancy. Blood and urine cultures are essential for identifying infections. A positive urine culture shows the growth of ≥100,000 colony-forming units/mL of urine. Positive blood cultures are found in 15–30% of cases. Peripheral blood film: May show leukocytosis with or without a left shift. Coagulation profile: Assessed when surgical intervention is planned. Miscellaneous tests: Include antinuclear antibody, perinuclear anti-neutrophil and cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil antibodies, protein C and S levels, Factor V Leiden mutation, anticardiolipin antibody (IgM and IgG), antithrombin III activity, vitamin B12, folic acid, and homocysteine levels to rule out other differential conditions, hypercoagulable states, and thromboembolic events. Radiographs (X-Ray) A plain abdominal film, also known as a KUB (kidney, ureter, bladder), can help identify urinary calculi. The entire film should be reviewed for intestinal gas patterns, gallstones, bony structures, and free air, which may provide insight into the etiology of the pain. Renal cell carcinomas: These osteolytic tumors may be visible radiographically in metastatic stages. Abnormal intestinal gas patterns, gallstones, or free air: Suggest intra-abdominal pathology. Aortic calcifications and aneurysms: Should be evaluated to determine if renal artery disease is causing flank pain. Urinary calculi: Appear as calcifications overlying the kidney shadow or along the ureter's course. Small stones (1–2 mm) can cause severe flank pain if they obstruct urinary flow into the bladder. Stones typically become obstructive at the ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, or at the ureterovesical junction (UVJ). Larger stones tend to lodge higher in the urinary tract. Uric acid calculi, being radiolucent, are not visible on plain abdominal films but can be detected via ultrasound or CT scan. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP) The IVP is a relatively inexpensive functional study that diagnoses most urologic, infectious, and cardiac causes of flank pain. Indication: When renal ultrasound and non-contrast CT scans do not assess renal function or when renal infarction due to arterial embolus is suspected, an IVP or intravenous contrast-enhanced CT scan may be performed to evaluate renal function. Contraindications: Include renal insufficiency, dehydration, prior reactions to iodinated contrast agents, and pregnancy. Adverse effects: The administration of iodine-based intravenous contrast medium may cause allergic reactions.
